q: A person has type B blood. What is on their red cells, and what is in their plasma?
options: B antigens; anti-B antibodies
A antigens; anti-B antibodies
B antigens; no ABO antibodies
B antigens; anti-A antibodies

why.correct: Type B red cells carry the B antigen, and the plasma holds antibodies against the ABO antigen the cells lack: anti-A.
options: Anti-B would attack the person's own red cells. The immune system does not make antibodies against its own antigens.
A antigens with anti-B antibodies describes type A.
Only type AB plasma lacks ABO antibodies.
Correct. B antigens, anti-A antibodies.

q: A typing test shows agglutination in the anti-A and anti-B wells and none in the anti-D well. What is the blood type?
options: O positive
AB negative
AB positive
O negative

why.correct: Clumping with anti-A and anti-B means the red cells carry both A and B antigens: type AB. No clumping with anti-D means no D antigen: Rh negative.
options: Type O cells carry neither A nor B, so they would not clump with anti-A or anti-B.
Correct. A and B present, D absent.
An Rh-positive sample would clump in the anti-D well too.
Type O cells would stay smooth in all three wells if Rh negative.

q: A patient is O positive. Which red cells can she safely receive?
options: O negative and O positive only
O positive only
Any Rh-positive type
O, A and B, as long as they are Rh positive

why.correct: Her plasma holds anti-A and anti-B, so she can receive only red cells with neither antigen: type O. As an Rh-positive person she makes no anti-D, so either Rh-positive or Rh-negative O cells are safe.
options: Correct. Only type O cells, of either Rh type.
O negative is also safe: it lacks the D antigen, which she already has.
A, B and AB red cells would meet her anti-A or anti-B.
Her anti-A and anti-B would attack A and B red cells whatever their Rh type.

q: A type A patient is mistakenly given a unit of type B red cells. Predict the change in each variable over the first hour, compared with before the transfusion.

variables.name: Agglutination of the donor red cells
variables.why: The patient's anti-B binds the B antigens on the donor cells and cross-links them into clumps.

variables.name: Free hemoglobin in the plasma
variables.why: Antibodies on the donor cells trigger plasma proteins that burst them, releasing hemoglobin into the plasma.

variables.name: Hemoglobin in the urine
variables.why: Free hemoglobin in the plasma is small enough to be filtered by the kidneys and spills into the urine, darkening it.

variables.name: Body temperature
variables.why: Chemical signals released during the antibody attack cause fever and chills.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: Signals released in the reaction widen blood vessels, so pressure falls and shock can follow.

why.correct: An ABO-incompatible transfusion sets off an immediate antibody attack on the donor cells. Agglutination and hemolysis release hemoglobin into the plasma and urine, and the reaction causes fever and a fall in blood pressure. The transfusion must be stopped at once.

q: Why can a person with AB positive blood receive red cells of any ABO and Rh type?
options: Their red cells carry every antigen, so donor cells cannot bind them
Their plasma has no anti-A, anti-B or anti-D to attack donor cells
Their immune system cannot make antibodies
Their plasma dilutes the donor's antibodies

why.correct: What matters is whether the recipient's plasma has antibodies against the donor cells' antigens. An AB-positive person already carries A, B and D, so they make antibodies against none of them.
options: Red cells do not bind other red cells. The danger comes from antibodies in the recipient's plasma.
Correct. No anti-A, anti-B or anti-D in the plasma.
Their immune system works normally; it simply makes no antibodies against antigens on its own cells.
Dilution of donor antibodies helps any recipient; it does not explain why AB positive accepts every red cell type.

q: A burn patient's blood type is unknown, and she needs plasma, not red cells. Which ABO type of plasma can be given without typing her first?
options: Type O
Type A
Type B
Type AB

why.correct: For plasma, the question is which antibodies the donor plasma carries. AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B, so it cannot attack the recipient's red cells, whatever her type. For plasma, AB is the universal donor.
options: Type O plasma holds anti-A and anti-B, which would attack the red cells of an A, B or AB recipient.
Type A plasma holds anti-B, which would attack B or AB red cells.
Type B plasma holds anti-A, which would attack A or AB red cells.
Correct. AB plasma carries no ABO antibodies.

misconception: Rh-negative people are born with anti-D
q: An Rh-negative man who has never had a transfusion is given Rh-positive, ABO-matched red cells in an emergency. What is most likely to happen?
options: An immediate, severe transfusion reaction
Nothing now, but he may make anti-D for next time
He becomes Rh positive permanently
Nothing now or later: Rh does not matter in men

why.correct: He has no anti-D yet, so the donor cells are not attacked at once. Over the next weeks his immune system may make anti-D against the D antigen he has met. A later Rh-positive transfusion could then trigger a reaction.
options: An immediate reaction needs antibodies already present. Anti-D forms only after exposure.
Correct. The first exposure sensitizes; the danger comes later.
Transfused cells live about 120 days at most; his own red cells stay Rh negative.
Rh matters for any future transfusion. In men there is no pregnancy risk, which is why O-positive blood is often used for men in emergencies.

q: An Rh-negative woman had an Rh-positive first baby three years ago and received no treatment. She is now pregnant with a second Rh-positive fetus, which becomes severely anemic before birth. What is the cause?
options: The fetus has inherited an enzyme defect from its father
The fetus's own antibodies attack its red cells
Her anti-A antibodies cross to the fetus
Anti-D from her first delivery destroys its red cells

why.correct: Fetal red cells entered her blood at the first delivery, and she made anti-D. That kind of antibody crosses from mother to fetus. In this Rh-positive fetus, it binds and destroys red cells: hemolytic disease of the newborn.
options: The history of a first Rh-positive baby without treatment points to maternal anti-D, not an inherited enzyme defect.
A fetus does not attack its own antigens; the antibodies come from the mother.
The problem here is Rh, not ABO, and most anti-A cannot cross to the fetus.
Correct. Maternal anti-D from the first pregnancy.

q: Why is a first Rh-positive baby of an Rh-negative mother usually unharmed?
options: Fetal cells enter her blood mostly at delivery
First babies have no D antigen until after birth
The mother's anti-D is destroyed during the first pregnancy
First babies have extra red cells that absorb the antibodies

why.correct: The bloods of mother and fetus normally stay apart, and most mixing happens at delivery. The mother then makes anti-D over the following weeks, after the baby has been born. The antibodies threaten the next Rh-positive pregnancy.
options: Correct. The timing of the first exposure protects the first baby.
Rh-positive fetuses carry the D antigen well before birth.
Before the first delivery she usually has no anti-D to destroy.
The protection comes from timing, not from extra red cells.

q: An Rh-negative woman has just delivered an Rh-positive baby. Why is she given an injection of anti-D immune globulin within 72 hours?
options: To give her newborn baby a supply of antibodies against infection
To clear fetal Rh-positive cells before she reacts to them
To turn her red cells Rh positive
To destroy any anti-D she already has

why.correct: The injected anti-D clears the fetal Rh-positive cells that entered her blood at delivery before her immune system responds to them, so she never starts making her own anti-D. The injected antibody is gone within months and does not harm later pregnancies.
options: The injection is for the mother, and it does not protect the baby against infection.
Correct. It prevents her from becoming sensitized.
Nothing changes her own red cells' Rh type.
Anti-D cannot destroy anti-D. Once she has made her own, the injection no longer helps.

q: A mother is type O and the father is type AB. Which blood types are possible for their children?
options: A or B
O only
AB only
A, B, AB or O

why.correct: The mother has two O copies and passes on an O. The father passes on either A or B. Children are therefore AO (type A) or BO (type B).
options: Correct. A or B, never AB or O.
A type O child needs an O copy from each parent; the AB father has none.
A type AB child needs an A from one parent and a B from the other; the mother can pass on only O.
O and AB are both impossible here.

q: A student says that when mismatched blood agglutinates, it is clotting. What is the key difference?
options: Agglutination needs platelets; clotting does not
Agglutination happens outside the body; clotting happens inside it
Antibodies clump cells in agglutination; fibrin forms a clot
There is no difference: they are two names for one and the same process

why.correct: Agglutination is an immune process: antibodies bind antigens on several cells and cross-link them into clumps. Coagulation is thrombin converting fibrinogen into fibrin threads. They can happen together in a severe transfusion reaction, but they are different processes.
options: Platelets are central to clotting, not to agglutination.
Agglutination happens inside the vessels in a transfusion reaction as well as in a typing test.
Correct. Different molecules, different mechanisms.
They involve different molecules and are triggered differently.

q: Put the steps in order to show how Rh antibodies harm a second Rh-positive fetus.
options: An Rh-negative mother carries her first Rh-positive fetus
At delivery, fetal Rh-positive red cells enter her blood
Over the following weeks she makes anti-D
In a later pregnancy, her anti-D crosses to an Rh-positive fetus
Anti-D binds the fetus's red cells, which are destroyed
The fetus becomes anemic, and bilirubin climbs after birth

why.correct: Exposure at the first delivery sensitizes the mother, who makes anti-D over weeks. In the next Rh-positive pregnancy, her anti-D crosses to the fetus and destroys its red cells, causing anemia and, after birth, rising bilirubin and jaundice.

q: A student described an ABO-incompatible transfusion reaction. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The recipient's antibodies bind antigens on the donor red cells
The donor cells agglutinate into clumps
The donor's plasma antibodies are the main cause of the damage
The donor cells burst, releasing hemoglobin into the plasma
Free hemoglobin darkens the urine

why.correct: The damage comes from the recipient's antibodies attacking the donor's red cells. Donor antibodies are few in a unit of packed red cells and are diluted in the recipient's large plasma volume.
options: This step is right. It starts the reaction.
This step is right. Antibodies cross-link the cells.
This is the error. The recipient's antibodies, not the donor's, cause the reaction.
This step is right. Hemolysis follows agglutination.
This step is right. Hemoglobin spills into the urine.

q: Complete the reading: a sample clumps with anti-B only, and stays smooth with anti-A and anti-D. Its type is ____.
options: A negative
B positive
B negative
O negative

why.correct: Clumping with anti-B shows the B antigen; no clumping with anti-A or anti-D shows no A and no D antigen. The type is B negative.
options: Type A cells would clump with anti-A, not anti-B.
An Rh-positive sample would also clump with anti-D.
Correct. B antigen only: B negative.
Type O cells would not clump with anti-B.

q: Use the chart. A type B patient needs red cells in an emergency. Which types does the chart list as compatible?
options: B and AB
A and O
B and O
Any type

why.correct: Type B plasma holds anti-A, so the donor cells must lack the A antigen: type B or type O.
options: AB red cells carry the A antigen, which the patient's anti-A would attack.
A cells carry the A antigen.
Correct. B and O cells both lack the A antigen.
Only an AB recipient can take any ABO type.

q: Compare the two enlarged panels. What is present in the second exposure that explains the harm to the fetus?
options: Maternal anti-Rh antibodies crossing into fetal blood
Many more fetal red cells leaking across into the mother's blood
A break in the barrier between the two bloods
Maternal red cells entering the fetus

why.correct: After the first exposure, the mother's blood holds many anti-Rh antibodies. In the second panel they cross into the fetal vessels and attach to the fetus's Rh-positive red cells.
options: Correct. The antibodies, made after the first exposure, cause the harm.
Fetal cells leaking into the mother cause the first exposure. The harm in the second pregnancy is done by antibodies moving the other way.
No break is needed in the second pregnancy; the antibodies cross an intact barrier.
The drawing shows antibodies, not maternal red cells, reaching the fetus.

q: A type O, Rh-positive mother gives birth to her first baby, who is type A and develops mild jaundice on day one. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Rh disease in a first-born baby
Some of her anti-A crossed to the fetus and destroyed a few of its red cells
The baby's own anti-B destroyed its red cells
Her anti-D attacked the baby's red cells

why.correct: A type O mother has anti-A and anti-B from infancy, with no earlier exposure needed. Most cannot reach the fetus, but a type O mother makes some that can. They bind the type A baby's red cells, and the destroyed cells raise bilirubin. ABO disease is usually mild because fetal cells carry A and B only weakly.
options: She is Rh positive, so she makes no anti-D; Rh disease is not possible.
Correct. Mild ABO hemolytic disease, which can occur in a first pregnancy.
The baby is type A and would not attack its own cells; newborns also make little anti-B yet.
An Rh-positive mother does not make anti-D.

q: Select every red cell transfusion that is compatible.
options: O negative cells to an AB positive patient
A positive cells to an A negative woman of childbearing age
B negative cells to an AB negative patient
AB positive cells to an O positive patient
O positive cells to a B positive patient

why.correct: Donor cells must not carry an antigen the recipient has, or will make, antibodies against. O negative cells suit anyone; B negative cells suit an AB negative patient, who has no anti-B and no D to meet; O positive cells suit a B positive patient.
options: Correct. O negative cells carry no A, B or D.
The D antigen would sensitize her, putting future pregnancies at risk.
Correct. B antigen is her own, and there is no D.
An O patient has anti-A and anti-B, which would attack AB red cells.
Correct. O cells carry no A or B, and she is already Rh positive.

q: A patient and a donor unit are both A positive. Why does the lab still crossmatch before the transfusion?
options: To check the donor's blood for anti-A
To confirm the unit's hemoglobin level
To detect antibodies against other blood groups
To make sure the donor cells are not actually type O

why.correct: ABO and Rh are only two of more than 40 blood group systems. A crossmatch mixes the patient's plasma with the donor's red cells; agglutination would reveal antibodies against another antigen on those cells.
options: A type A donor has no anti-A; the concern is the recipient's plasma meeting the donor's cells.
A crossmatch tests compatibility, not hemoglobin.
Correct. It catches incompatibilities beyond ABO and Rh.
The unit's type is already known; a crossmatch looks for reactions, not type.
